In [[mathematics]], '''Dvoretzky's theorem''' is an important structural theorem about [[normed vector space]]s proved by [[Aryeh Dvoretzky]] in the early 1960s,<ref>{{Cite book |first=A. |last=Dvoretzky |chapter=Some results on convex bodies and Banach spaces |year=1961 |title=Proc. Internat. Sympos. Linear Spaces (Jerusalem, 1960) |pages=123–160 |publisher=Jerusalem Academic Press |location=Jerusalem }}</ref> answering a question of [[Alexander Grothendieck]]. In essence, it says that every sufficiently high-dimensional normed vector space will have low-dimensional subspaces that are approximately [[Euclidean space|Euclidean]]. Equivalently, every high-dimensional bounded symmetric [[convex set]] has low-dimensional sections that are approximately [[ellipsoid]]s.

A new proof found by [[Vitali Milman]] in the 1970s<ref>{{Cite journal |first=V. D. |last=Milman |title=A new proof of A. Dvoretzky's theorem on cross-sections of convex bodies |language=ru |journal=Funkcional. Anal. I Prilozhen. |volume=5 |year=1971 |issue=4 |pages=28–37 }}</ref> was one of the starting points for the development of [[asymptotic geometric analysis]] (also called ''asymptotic [[functional analysis]]'' or the ''local theory of Banach spaces'').<ref>{{Cite book |quote=The full significance of measure concentration was first realized by Vitali Milman in his revolutionary proof [Mil1971] of the theorem of Dvoretzky ... Dvoretzky's theorem, especially as proved by Milman, is a milestone in the local (that is, finite-dimensional) theory of Banach spaces.  While I feel sorry for a mathematician who cannot see its intrinsic appeal, this appeal on its own does not explain the enormous influence that the proof has had, well beyond Banach space theory, as a result of planting the idea of measure concentration in the minds of many mathematicians.  Huge numbers of papers have now been published exploiting this idea or giving new techniques for showing that it holds. |first=W. T. |last=Gowers |chapter=The two cultures of mathematics |title=Mathematics: frontiers and perspectives |pages=65–78 |publisher=Amer. Math. Soc. |location=Providence, RI |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8218-2070-4 }}</ref>

==Original formulations==
For every natural number ''k''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;'''N''' and every ''&epsilon;''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 there exists a natural number ''N''(''k'',&nbsp;''&epsilon;'')&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;'''N''' such that if (''X'',&nbsp;‖·‖) is any normed space of dimension ''N''(''k'',&nbsp;''&epsilon;''), there exists a subspace ''E''&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;''X'' of dimension ''k'' and a positive definite [[quadratic form]] ''Q'' on ''E'' such that the corresponding Euclidean norm

:<math>| \cdot | = \sqrt{Q(\cdot)} </math>

on ''E'' satisfies:

:<math> |x| \leq \|x\| \leq (1+\varepsilon)|x| \quad \text{for every} \ x \in E.</math>
In terms of the [[Banach–Mazur compactum|multiplicative Banach-Mazur distance ''d'']] the theorem's conclusion can be formulated as:

:<math>d(E,\ \ell_k^2)\leq 1+\varepsilon </math>

where <math>\ell_k^2</math> denotes the standard ''k''-dimensional Euclidean space.

Since the [[Unit sphere|unit ball]] of every normed vector space is a bounded, symmetric, convex set and the unit ball of every Euclidean space is an ellipsoid, the theorem may also be formulated as a statement about ellipsoid sections of convex sets.

As a consequence, we have the following statement. For any <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, we call a <math>\epsilon</math>-sphere a convex body <math>K</math> such that there exists a ball <math>B</math>, such that <math>B \subset K \subset (1 + \epsilon) B</math>. Then, for any integer <math>n</math> and any <math>\epsilon \in (0, 1)</math>, for all large enough <math>N</math>, and any <math>N</math>-dimensional centrally symmetric body, there exists an <math>n</math>-dimensional subspace <math>V \subset \R^N</math>, such that <math>K \cap V</math> is an <math>\epsilon</math>-sphere.<ref>{{Citation |last=Zong |first=Chuanming |chapter=Dvoretzky’s Theorem |date=1996 |title=Strange Phenomena in Convex and Discrete Geometry |pages=123–142 |editor-last=Dudziak |editor-first=James J. |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4613-8481-6_7 |access-date=2025-05-28 |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer New York |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-8481-6_7 |isbn=978-0-387-94734-1 |last2=Dudziak |first2=James J.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Further developments==

In 1971, [[Vitali Milman]] gave a new proof of Dvoretzky's theorem, making use of the [[concentration of measure]] on the sphere to show that a random ''k''-dimensional subspace satisfies the above inequality with probability very close to 1. The proof gives the sharp dependence on ''k'':

:<math>N(k,\varepsilon)\leq\exp(C(\varepsilon)k)</math>

where the constant ''C''(''&epsilon;'') only depends on ''&epsilon;''.

We can thus state: for every ''&epsilon;''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 there exists a constant C(&epsilon;) > 0 such that for every normed space (''X'',&nbsp;‖·‖) of dimension ''N'', there exists a subspace ''E''&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;''X'' of dimension
''k''&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;''C''(''&epsilon;'')&nbsp;log&nbsp;''N'' and a Euclidean norm |&sdot;| on ''E'' such that 
:<math> |x| \leq \|x\| \leq (1+\varepsilon)|x| \quad \text{for every} \ x \in E.</math>

More precisely, let ''S''<sup>''N''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1</sup> denote the unit sphere with respect to some Euclidean structure ''Q'' on ''X'', and let ''&sigma;'' be the invariant probability measure on ''S''<sup>''N''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1</sup>. Then:
* there exists such a subspace ''E'' with

:: <math>k = \dim E \geq C(\varepsilon) \, \left(\frac{\int_{S^{N-1}} \| \xi \| \, d\sigma(\xi)}{\max_{\xi \in S^{N-1}} \| \xi \|}\right)^2 \, N.  </math>

* For any ''X'' one may choose ''Q'' so that the term in the brackets will be at most

:: <math> c_1 \sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N}}.</math>

Here ''c''<sub>1</sub> is a universal constant. For given ''X'' and ''&epsilon;'', the largest possible ''k'' is denoted ''k''<sub>*</sub>(''X'') and called the [[Dvoretzky dimension]] of ''X''.

The dependence on ''&epsilon;'' was studied by [[Yehoram Gordon]],<ref>{{Cite journal |first=Y. |last=Gordon |title=Some inequalities for Gaussian processes and applications |journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=50 |year=1985 |issue=4 |pages=265–289 |doi= 10.1007/bf02759761|doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |first=Y. |last=Gordon |title=Gaussian processes and almost spherical sections of convex bodies |journal=Annals of Probability |volume=16 |year=1988 |issue=1 |pages=180–188 |doi= 10.1214/aop/1176991893|doi-access=free }}</ref> who showed that ''k''<sub>*</sub>(''X'')&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;''c''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;''&epsilon;''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;log&nbsp;''N''. Another proof of this result was given by [[Gideon Schechtman]].<ref>{{Cite book |first=G. |last=Schechtman|author-link=Gideon Schechtman |chapter=A remark concerning the dependence on ε in Dvoretzky's theorem |title=Geometric aspects of functional analysis (1987–88) |pages=274–277 |series=Lecture Notes in Math. |volume=1376 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin |year=1989 |isbn=978-0-387-51303-4 }}</ref>

[[Noga Alon]] and [[Vitali Milman]] showed that the logarithmic bound on the dimension of the subspace in Dvoretzky's theorem can be significantly improved, if one is willing to accept a subspace that is close either to a Euclidean space or to a [[Chebyshev distance|Chebyshev space]]. Specifically, for some constant ''c'', every ''n''-dimensional space has a subspace of dimension ''k''&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;exp(''c''{{radic|log&nbsp;''N''}}) that is close either to ''ℓ''{{su|b=2|p=''k''}} or to ''ℓ''{{su|b=&infin;|p=''k''}}.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Alon | first1 = N. | author1-link = Noga Alon
 | last2 = Milman | first2 = V. D. | author2-link = Vitali Milman
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02804012 | doi-access=
 | mr = 720303
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]
 | pages = 265–280
 | title = Embedding of <math>\scriptstyle \ell^k_\infty</math> in finite-dimensional Banach spaces
 | volume = 45
 | year = 1983}}.</ref>

Important related results were proved by [[Tadeusz Figiel]], [[Joram Lindenstrauss]] and Milman.<ref>{{Cite journal |first=T. |last=Figiel |first2=J. |last2=Lindenstrauss |first3=V. D. |last3=Milman |title=The dimension of almost spherical sections of convex bodies |journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=82 |year=1976 |issue=4 |pages=575–578 |doi= 10.1090/s0002-9904-1976-14108-0|doi-access=free }}, expanded in 
"The dimension of almost spherical sections of convex bodies",
Acta Math. '''139''' (1977), 53&ndash;94.</ref>
